candidates.title: Accuracy of artificial intelligence models integrating machine learning and deep learning in detecting microvascular invasion in liver cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
candidates.abstract: e16184 Background: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a global health challenge, ranking sixth in incidence and third in cancer-related mortality. Microvascular invasion (MVI) is a crucial prognostic marker influencing recurrence rates and survival. Accurate preoperative MVI detection can guide surgical planning but is limited by invasive histopathological exams and interobserver variability. This study evaluates the diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence (AI) models, including machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), in predicting MVI in HCC using imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, ultrasound, PET/CT, and histopathology. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines, covering studies from 2010 to 2023. Comprehensive searches were conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, European PMC, and BioMed Central. AI models were assessed for diagnostic accuracy using QUADAS-2 and Radiomics Quality Score (RQS). Metrics like the area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity were analyzed. Results: This meta-analysis synthesized data from 51 studies, encompassing 6,257 records. DL models showed a pooled AUC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.80–0.86), with sensitivity and specificity of 0.79 (95% CI: 0.75–0.82) and 0.84 (95% CI: 0.79–0.88), respectively. ML models achieved a pooled AUC of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.80–0.86), sensitivity of 0.79 (95% CI: 0.71–0.85), and higher specificity of 0.88 (95% CI: 0.84–0.92). Across imaging modalities, MRI and CT-based models achieved pooled AUCs of 0.87 and 0.83 for DL and 0.85 and 0.82 for ML, respectively. Ultrasound-based models demonstrated higher specificity but slightly lower sensitivity. Models incorporating clinical features did not outperform purely radiomics-based approaches. Quality assessments revealed low bias risks in patient selection (88%), index tests (94%), and reference standards (98%). However, only 51% of studies addressed inter-scanner variability, and 55% incorporated calibration or resampling. The mean RQS was 40%, with 84% adhering to robust imaging protocols. Conclusions: AI models, particularly DL, exhibit robust accuracy in predicting MVI in HCC, showing promise for integration into clinical workflows. These tools could enable personalized preoperative planning, improving patient outcomes and reducing recurrence risks. Standardized protocols, prospective validation, and broader adoption of advanced AI methods are needed to ensure consistent clinical utility and cost-effectiveness.

candidates.title: Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI deep learning model combined with clinical model for noninvasive differentiation of hepatocellular carcinoma from mass-forming intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma
candidates.abstract: Rationale and objectives This study aims to develop a framework integrating dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI)-based multi-channel deep learning combined with clinical modeling for the non-invasive preoperative discrimination between hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and mass-forming intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (MF-ICC). Methods The internal development cohort comprised 334 surgically confirmed patients, including 231 patients with HCC and 103 with MF-ICC, and was divided at the patient level into a training cohort ( n = 233) and an internal validation cohort ( n = 101). The independent external validation cohort included 50 patients, comprising 40 with HCC and 10 with MF-ICC. We constructed separate two-dimensional deep learning models based on arterial phase, portal venous phase, and delayed phase images and then developed fusion models (2D model). A multi-channel deep learning model was further developed by directly inputting the three-phase images stacked along the channel dimension. Moreover, a clinical model was built based on independent predictors identified through multivariate analysis, which was ultimately integrated with the best-performing deep learning model. Model performance was evaluated and compared. Results Deep learning model directly feeding the three-phase images as a multi-channel input achieved better discrimination (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.814 in the internal validation cohort) than all single-phase and corresponding fusion models. The comprehensive 2D + multi-channel + clinical model showed the best performance for the differentiation of HCC from MF-ICC, achieving an AUC of 0.887 (95% CI, 0.819–0.954) in the internal validation cohort, and generalized well to the external validation cohort (AUC = 0.908; 95% CI, 0.811–1.000). However, no significant differences in AUCs were found among the models after correction for multiple comparisons. Conclusion The fusion model integrating clinical predictors with DCE-MRI multi-phase deep learning feature may provide a valuable tool for preoperatively differentiating HCC from MF-ICC.

candidates.title: Preoperative prediction of HCC microvascular invasion by multimodel peritumoral diffusion MRI
candidates.abstract: Abstract Objective Most studies emphasize intratumoral diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) metrics, but few studies have examined whether peritumoral DWI metrics can provide added value. We aimed to evaluate three-dimensional, multiscale, multimodel DWI parameters within intratumoral and peritumoral volumes of interest for predicting microvascular invasion (MVI) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Materials and methods Seventy patients with HCC, including 42 with MVI, were prospectively enrolled. We calculated parameters from monoexponential, intravoxel incoherent motion, diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), stretched-exponential model (SEM), and continuous-time random-walk models within the tumor and in 3-mm (P3) and 5-mm (P5) peritumoral rims. Features showing differences on univariable analysis were further screened using logistic regression with variance inflation factor filtering to build combined models. Diagnostic performance was assessed by areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Results Four intratumoral diffusion-coefficient–related metrics showed significant differences between groups. In the peritumoral regions, 12 parameters differed between groups, including diffusion-coefficient–related indices and heterogeneity-related metrics. Among single parameters, P3_DKI_ K app achieved the best discrimination for MVI (AUROC = 0.713); P5_DKI_ K app and Tumor_SEM_DDC were selected as independent imaging predictors. After integrating alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and tumor size, the combined model (Cli-IntraPeriDWI) yielded the best performance (AUROC = 0.844). SHAP analysis indicated that higher AFP, larger tumor size, higher P5_DKI_ K app , and lower Tumor_SEM_DDC were associated with increased MVI risk. Conclusion Peritumoral DWI offers multiple biomarkers and outperforms intratumoral metrics for MVI prediction. An interpretable model integrating peritumoral and intratumoral DWI with clinical factors enables accurate, noninvasive preoperative MVI risk stratification in HCC. Key Points Question Can multiscale, multimodel peritumoral DWI metrics improve preoperative prediction of MVI in HCC compared with intratumoral DWI metrics? Findings Compared with intratumoral DWI, peritumoral DWI offered more potential imaging biomarkers and superior diagnostic capability for the preoperative diagnosis of MVI in HCC. Relevance statement By integrating intratumoral and peritumoral metrics with clinical risk factors, we developed a model achieving optimal performance and transparent decision interpretability for MVI assessment, supporting preoperative prognostic evaluation and individualized treatment planning in HCC.

candidates.title: Preoperative prediction of microvascular invasion in small hepatocellular carcinoma (≤ 3 cm) by leveraging cross-phase variations of MRI contrast phases
candidates.abstract: Abstract Purpose Noninvasive preoperative prediction of microvascular invasion (MVI) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a significant clinical challenge worldwide. This study encoded feature variations across multi-phase MRI sequences for the preoperative prediction of MVI. Method Data were retrospectively examined for 115 consecutive patients (mean age: 57.2 ± 10.7 years; 95 men) who had undergone surgical resection for HCC (tumor diameter less than 3 cm). All of them underwent preoperative MR examination and were randomly partitioned into training and testing cohorts at an 8:2 ratio. Peritumoral expansions (3 mm, 5 mm, and 10 mm) were generated from manually segmented intratumoral regions of interest (ROIs) across the arterial, venous, and delayed phases. Radiomics features were subsequently extracted from both the original and expanded ROIs. We then evaluated the predictive performance of five encoding methods combined with four machine learning classifiers using both clinical characteristics and radiomics features. Result Multi-phase models incorporating temporal encoding methods consistently outperformed single-phase models and those relying solely on clinical characteristics. Among all evaluated combinations, the Fourier-inspired temporal encoding method combined with an ExtraTrees classifier, applied to the original tumoral ROI with a 5-mm peritumoral expansion, achieved the best diagnostic performance, with an AUC of 0.850 (95% CI: 0.675–0.978). Conclusion While radiologists routinely monitor multi-phase contrast dynamics qualitatively, our findings demonstrate that these cross-phase variations provide quantifiable, highly predictive information for MVI. This framework represents a promising, noninvasive quantitative tool for preoperative MVI risk stratification.

candidates.title: A multiparametric liver MRI dataset with multiple tumor and liver segmentations of pre-treatment hepatocellular carcinomas
candidates.abstract: Abstract Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary liver cancer and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. While dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) plays a key role for HCC screening, diagnosis and treatment planning, the development of AI models for detection and characterization of focal liver lesions is hindered by the scarcity of publicly available annotated MRI datasets. Here, we present OpenSwissHCC, a curated multiphasic dataset of 132 multiparametric DCE-MRI scans from adult patients with chronic liver disease acquired on 1.5 T and 3 T MRI scanners between 2011 and 2020. The dataset includes both HCC-positive (n = 63) and HCC-negative (n = 69) patients, with up to five lesions per patient segmented across each sequence when confidently identified. Whole-liver and lesion segmentations were manually performed and expert-validated, with lesion metadata including LI-RADS scores, size, liver segment location, major LI-RADS imaging features (non-rim APHE, washout, capsule, threshold growth) and key ancillary/background findings (e.g., mosaic architecture, fat/blood products, necrosis, tumor-in-vein; cirrhosis and portal-hypertension signs). In total, 140 lesions were annotated, including 97 confirmed HCC. Additionally, we provide liver masks for all T1-weighted images (T1-WI) sequences, generated using a pre-trained nnU-Net model, as well as pre-computed transforms to facilitate registration across T1-WI phases. By providing a comprehensive, well-annotated, and standardized collection of liver MRI examinations, OpenSwissHCC aims to assist the development and benchmarking of advanced computational methods for automated HCC detection, segmentation, and characterization, fostering progress toward precision imaging and personalized treatment planning.

candidates.title: Head-to-head comparison of [18F]FAPI and [18F]FDG PET/CT in the clinical value of hepatocellular carcinoma
candidates.abstract: To investigate the clinical utility of fluorine-18-labeled fibroblast activation protein (FAP) inhibitor ([ 18 F]FAPI) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) relative to [ 18 F]fluorodeoxyglucose ([ 18 F]FDG) PET/CT for tumor detection and staging in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients. A cohort of 38 individuals (median age, 61 years; interquartile range, 56–68 years), all with pathologically confirmed primary or recurrent HCC, were enrolled. All participants underwent both [ 18 F]FDG and [ 18 F]FAPI PET/CT. Maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax), tumor-to-background ratio (TBR), metabolic tumor volume (MTV), FAP expression tumor volume (FTV), total lesion glycolysis (TLG), total lesion FAP expression (TLF), and clinical staging were compared. Each patient had at least one intrahepatic lesion confirmed by surgical resection or percutaneous biopsy. Histopathologic confirmation was available for 46/66 intrahepatic lesions, 3/56 lymph-node (LN) metastases, and 4/33 distant metastases; the remaining lesions were adjudicated using a composite reference standard based on multimodal imaging follow-up and treatment response. Additionally, correlations between PET imaging findings and serum biomarkers, comprising alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and protein induced by vitamin K absence or antagonist II (PIVKA-II), were analyzed. The cohort included 32 primary and 6 recurrent HCC cases. [ 18 F]FAPI PET/CT showed higher lesion detection rates than [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT for primary intrahepatic lesions (96.7% vs. 60.0%; p < 0.001), LN metastases (94.6% vs. 80.4%; p = 0.021), and distant metastases (78.8% vs. 48.5%; p = 0.002). For primary intrahepatic lesions, [ 18 F]FAPI PET/CT showed higher SUVmax (7.90 vs. 4.80, p < 0.001) and TBR (5.45 vs. 2.60, p < 0.001) than [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT. In the patient-level volumetric analysis of the 32 initial-staging patients, FTV was 21.04 vs. MTV 13.75 ( p < 0.001), and TLF was 135.36 vs. TLG 51.44 ( p < 0.001). For LN metastases, [ 18 F]FAPI PET/CT showed higher SUVmax (7.98 vs. 6.63, p = 0.048) and TBR (7.85 vs. 4.95, p < 0.001), as well as higher FTV than MTV (6.55 vs. 4.55, p < 0.001) and TLF than TLG (67.65 vs. 52.75, p < 0.001). Positive correlations were observed between [ 18 F]FAPI PET/CT tumor uptake parameters and AFP and PIVKA-II levels (nominal p < 0.05). Relative to [ 18 F]FDG, [ 18 F]FAPI PET/CT produced staging changes in 19/32 patients undergoing initial staging, including 6 true upstagings, and identified 3 additional local recurrences; a FAPI-informed management change was implemented in 57.9% (22/38) of patients. Exploratory receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.947, 0.921, 0.895, and 0.864 for SUVmax, TBR, FTV, and TLF, respectively. [ 18 F]FAPI PET/CT showed higher lesion detection in selected HCC settings than [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT for primary intrahepatic, lymph-node, and distant metastatic lesions and may provide complementary information for staging and treatment planning in this preliminary single-center cohort. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05810324; registered on 30 March 2023.

candidates.title: Foundation Model‐Enabled Pathology‐Informed MRI Model for Preoperative Prediction of Vessels Encapsulating Tumor Clusters in Resectable Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Multicenter Retrospective Study
candidates.abstract: Vessels encapsulating tumor clusters (VETC) are an aggressive vascular phenotype of hepatocellular carcinoma that is usually determined after surgery. A foundation model-enabled framework for pathology-informed VETC prediction on pretreatment magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), termed PIVOT, uses paired preoperative multiparametric MRI, postoperative hematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images, and CD34 immunohistochemistry during model development, while inference requires only preoperative MRI. PIVOT-MRI uses morphologic and vascular embedding alignment, and PIVOT-Clinical combines the PIVOT-MRI score with tumor size and alpha-fetoprotein. The multicenter retrospective study includes 2052 patients in a training cohort, an internal test cohort, and four external validation cohorts. PIVOT-MRI achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.887 in the internal test cohort and 0.839-0.861 across external cohorts. PIVOT-Clinical increases the internal-test area under the curve to 0.904 and PIVOT-Clinical-defined groups are associated with different two-year recurrence risks. Removing both histopathologic alignment branches results in the largest ablation-related performance decrease. Exploratory radiotranscriptomic analyses showed that higher PIVOT-MRI scores were associated with angiogenesis-related, endothelial, and proliferative transcriptional programs. PIVOT enables noninvasive preoperative assessment of pathology-defined vascular aggressiveness in resectable hepatocellular carcinoma while preserving an MRI-only clinical inference pathway.

candidates.title: Combined analysis of preoperative circulating tumor cells status and tumor size to guide width of resection margin for solitary hepatocellular carcinoma
candidates.abstract: Background The optimal resection margin width for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains controversial. The purpose of this study was to explore the value of preoperative circulating tumor cells (CTCs) status and tumor size in guiding the resection margin width of patients with HCC. Methods This study was a multicenter retrospective study that included 383 patients who underwent resection of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Preoperative circulating tumor cell (CTC) detection (CTC ≥ 1/CTC = 0) and imaging evaluation of tumor size (≤ 3 cm/> 3 cm) were performed in all patients. We aimed to compare recurrence-free survival (RFS) and overall survival (OS) between patients receiving narrow (< 1 cm) and wide (≥ 1 cm) resection margins. Results Tumor diameter and CTC status were independent predictors of RFS and OS in the entire cohort. In patients with tumor diameter ≤ 3 cm, CTC-positive status correlated with poorer RFS but not OS. RFS and OS of narrow margin group and wide margin group were similar, and there was no statistical significance (P > 0.05). In the patients with tumor diameter > 3 cm and CTC-negative group, the RFS and OS of the narrow margin group were comparable to those of the wide margin group (P > 0.05). However, in patients with tumor diameter > 3 cm and CTC-positive groups, RFS and OS were better in the wide margin group than in the narrow margin group (P < 0.05). Conclusions Using preoperative CTC status and tumor diameter as preoperative markers, combined analysis of CTC status and tumor diameter could help to determine surgical margin width in patients with solitary HCC. Narrow margins are indicated for patients with a tumor diameter ≤ 3 cm (regardless of CTC status) and for patients with a tumor diameter > 3 cm and CTC-negative. Whereas wide margins are preferred in patients with tumors > 3 cm in diameter and CTC-positive.

candidates.title: Surgical resection combined with TACE for primary clear cell carcinoma of the liver: a case report and literature review
candidates.abstract: Background Primary clear cell carcinoma of the liver (PCCCL) is an uncommon hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) subtype that resembles extrahepatic clear cell tumors, posing diagnostic challenges. Case presentation A 74-year-old woman with hepatitis B–related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class A) presented with acute abdominal pain and vomiting. Imaging revealed a hypervascular hepatic lesion with intralesional fat, while serum AFP was normal and CA125 mildly elevated. Laparoscopic partial hepatectomy was performed. Histology confirmed PCCCL, and immunohistochemistry supported hepatic origin while excluding metastatic renal carcinoma. The patient subsequently received two sessions of postoperative TACE as an individualized treatment and remained free of recurrence or metastasis during surveillance from 2022 to 2025. Conclusion PCCCL is rare and difficult to distinguish from conventional HCC or metastatic clear cell carcinoma. Histopathology with immunohistochemistry is essential for diagnosis. Surgical resection is the mainstay of treatment. Although this patient remained recurrence-free after postoperative TACE, the role of TACE cannot be determined based on a single case, and studies with larger sample sizes are still needed.
